title: Fannin County Folk and Fact, Page 61 — Savoy College and private schools
text:
In 1881 the Masonic Female Institute was established in Bonham. The Masonic Lodge had sponsored schools during the years since it had begun in the 1840's, both in Bonham and Honey Grove. The Institute was a school whose students not only from Bonham and the surrounding area, but the Carlton College of Honey Grove students attended as well as West Texas. Both of the girls' schools stressed classical education, emphasizing the academic and musical subjects.

The third private school in Bonham during this period was Fannin College, incorporated in 1883 for boys only. On the same campus was the Lyceum, which was the boys' auditorium, which was attended by boys and girls together until they reached a certain age. Boys who completed their studies at Lyceum were expected to continue at Fannin College or the neighboring Carlton College. The boys were expected to continue at Carlton College or similar institution.

One who attended the Lyceum School in the 1880's remembered about having a cistern on the yard of the junior who was in it. It was equipped with a large stove with pot-bellied stone burning coal. Sometimes the stove would smoke and the children would sleep or stay over it until the janitor could fix it. Lyceum was a two-story frame building with the recitation rooms downstairs and the ninth and tenth grades upstairs." This information is from an interview in the Bonham paper, November 17, 1952.

The purpose for which these schools were functioning is also an example of differentiation and integration of formal schooling in the region. In Ladonia there were three schools: Featherstone School of Dallas — an academic institution — which was boarding school. It made Ladonia a desirable place for settlers coming with their families. And after the Civil War, in 1909 Ladonia had a school called Farmers Improvement Society, which was an organization for the Black community.

During the 1850's the Masonic Lodge in Honey Grove opened convenient schools in an old Masonic Lodge building. They rented or owned a two-story building of the Methodist Church built the Paris District Honey Grove school and by 1885 had 8,000 books. Honey Grove continued to be used as a school even after lack of funds caused the closing of the Masonic Lodge facility. The Old Masonic Hall School was operated mainly as a boys' school. The school was a large private school for business, this building became part of the public schools. An Old Masonic Hall school was a large private school for accounting, bookkeeping, language and literature, civic selections, mathematical studies, shorthand and penmanship — "taking ad-vantages" of instrumental and vocal music.

This advertisement from the Dodd City High School:

"The course of study is thoroughly classical and practical. All pupils who desire to comply with state regulations must regularly attend. Pupils who have been irregular are not wanted at any terms."

1. From High School catalog of 1895-96 stated the regulations governing the pupils in the school: '1) There shall be no association of males and females. If the teachers see fit to suspend the rules. 2) Students are required to attend all exercises. No use of obscene language is forbidden. 4) Any student wilfully associated in the breaking of any rule or the school regulations shall be accounted accessory to the offender and shall be dealt with in the same as the offender. 5) There shall be no secret societies. 6) Students in the third year and above for any reason shall have their conditions will be dropped to the next lower grade.' "The grades in the English course were to be English in two classes — differential and integral calculus and mathematical astronomy. Four years of English were required of all students taking English courses. Texas and U.S. history, government and economics were required of all students along with a wide range of academic curriculum.

A boarding school, as well as a day school was Savoy Male and Female College, which came from the various parts of the county and from out of state. Medals were awarded for various accomplishments. A medal was awarded for spelling excellence during the session.

The Savoy Male and Female College influenced the lives and hundreds of young men and women during the years before. As required by the Lyceum School and the other private schools, it had periods of financial uncertainty. The years 1876-1895 saw the school in its greatest era of growth. From 1884-1895 Professor Halsell, the president, encouraged a closer relationship between the school and Indian Territory provided a means for the education of Choctaw and Chickasaw students enrolled in the school. In other boarding schools, Liberal subsidies of $20 per month were granted by the two main Indian nations — the Choctaw and Chickasaw tribes who were settled in southern Oklahoma. These subsidies made the school prosperous and self-supporting. The charter was obtained in 1880.

Private schools were conducted in numerous rural communities in the county, including Dodd City, Ladonia, Ravenna, Bells and Dial. Such schools were designed to give more advanced instruction at the rural level. Many had probably been established in the 1880's. Children in the rural communities were under the shared administration of the county judge, acting as the county superintendent of schools. A judge would be responsible for inspecting and certifying the credentials of the teachers and registering pupils. For the year 1885 a $5.30 per child apportionment was given to the total enrollment in county schools for six months. At one time there was a total of 172 rural schools in Fannin County and an additional 40 schools for the colored children. Many of these rural schools had one teacher with an average of about twenty children per pupil.

Many of the rural private schools in Fannin County during this period had full academic programs. The Savoy Male and Female College during its most prosperous years brought many young men and women to the West to obtain an education not available locally. It was one of the finest private schools for any capable, talented, well-educated persons in the late nineteenth century in Texas. Those who played piano or stringed instruments had full classes. Drawing, china painting, weaving and water colors were also offered.
notes: This is page 61 from 'Fannin County Folk and Fact' (1977), a local history book. Includes a photograph in the upper right of what appears to be a classroom or school building setting (partially visible, students at desks). Dodd City High School catalog excerpt is quoted directly. The section on Savoy Male and Female College is the most relevant Savoy-specific content and has been transcribed fully. Other sections describe the general private school landscape of Fannin County. Text is dense and some passages are partially obscured by image quality.
